chapters.title: Can you get an MIT education without going to MIT?
chapters.sourcePressure: Self-directed learning becomes serious when the learner borrows a real standard, sets a fixed clock, and defines evidence before comfort can edit the goal.
chapters.coreMove: Turn a vague self-education wish into a benchmarked mission that can be judged by external proof.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating the MIT Challenge as a stunt, productivity flex, or anti-college argument instead of a design lesson about mission, benchmark, and proof.

chapters.title: Why ultralearning matters
chapters.sourcePressure: The chapter contrasts ultralearning with dabbling and frames rapid adaptation, focused effort, and weakness-first work as a response to changing conditions.
chapters.coreMove: Decide when a hard skill deserves protected intensity instead of being left as casual exploration.
chapters.commonMisread: Saying every interest should become a high-pressure project or that intensity alone beats thoughtful exploration.

chapters.title: How to become an ultralearner
chapters.sourcePressure: First projects should focus on one thing, use clear constraints, choose a full-time, fixed-schedule, or fixed-hour format, and run preparation through a pilot week.
chapters.coreMove: Convert ambition into one constrained project format, then test the plan with a pilot before committing fully.
chapters.commonMisread: Skipping straight from excitement to an oversized plan with no test of schedule, materials, or first week reality.

chapters.title: Principle 1: Metalearning: first draw a map
chapters.sourcePressure: Metalearning researches purpose, skill components, and methods before and during a project so effort has direction without becoming rigid.
chapters.coreMove: Map why, what, and how before sprinting, then revise the map when the project teaches back.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning mapping into endless research or a fixed recipe that keeps the learner away from the skill.

chapters.title: Principle 2: Focus: sharpen your knife
chapters.sourcePressure: Focus concerns starting, sustaining, and protecting concentration from interruption without making the setup itself the performance.
chapters.coreMove: Remove start friction and attention leakage so demanding work gets real contact time.
chapters.commonMisread: Reducing focus to aesthetics, timers, or heroic willpower while the task never gets uninterrupted contact.

chapters.title: Principle 3: Directness: go straight ahead
chapters.sourcePressure: Directness means practicing in the real context of the target skill and increasing transfer by reducing distance from actual use.
chapters.coreMove: Move practice toward the actual performance arena instead of hiding inside comfortable proxies.
chapters.commonMisread: Assuming more preparation is automatically useful even when it never resembles the target performance.

chapters.title: Principle 4: Drill: attack your weakest point
chapters.sourcePressure: Drill isolates a bottleneck that whole-task practice is too coarse to fix, but the fragment must feed back into performance.
chapters.coreMove: Find the rate-limiting weakness, isolate it briefly, then reconnect it to the whole skill.
chapters.commonMisread: Practicing the easiest fragment or treating drills as detached exercises that never return to the real task.

chapters.title: Principle 5: Retrieval: test to learn
chapters.sourcePressure: Retrieval means producing knowledge through recall instead of smoothing over weakness with passive rereading.
chapters.coreMove: Force knowledge out from memory before looking again, so testing becomes learning rather than judgment.
chapters.commonMisread: Framing retrieval as exam anxiety, trivia, or punishment instead of a way to expose what the page was hiding.

chapters.title: Principle 6: Feedback: Don't dodge the punches
chapters.sourcePressure: Feedback means exposing work to useful correction instead of protecting errors because correction feels uncomfortable.
chapters.coreMove: Put imperfect work where correction can hit it while there is still time to adjust.
chapters.commonMisread: Treating all criticism as equally wise or turning feedback into generic praise and blame.

chapters.title: Principle 7: Retention: Don't fill a leaky bucket
chapters.sourcePressure: Retention addresses fast forgetting and the need to revisit important material after one successful encounter.
chapters.coreMove: Protect important gains with planned returns before fluent work quietly leaks away.
chapters.commonMisread: Trying to preserve everything forever or assuming one good session locks a skill in place.

chapters.title: Principle 8: Intuition: Dig deep before building up
chapters.sourcePressure: Intuition emphasizes deep understanding before adding knowledge, so later material rests on grasp rather than surface familiarity.
chapters.coreMove: Pause at shallow understanding and dig into why the step works before stacking more material on top.
chapters.commonMisread: Making intuition mystical, anti-practice, or simply a feeling of confidence.

chapters.title: Principle 9: Experimentation: Explore outside your comfort zone
chapters.sourcePressure: Experimentation pushes beyond default methods and comfort-zone habits while staying tied to the real skill.
chapters.coreMove: Test a meaningful alternative to the default method when comfort stops revealing new information.
chapters.commonMisread: Changing methods randomly, chasing novelty, or assuming discomfort proves improvement.

chapters.title: Your first ultralearning project
chapters.sourcePressure: A first project should be hard enough to matter, concrete enough to guide action, and protected enough to compete for time.
chapters.coreMove: Choose a first project serious enough to deserve protected time and small enough to start cleanly.
chapters.commonMisread: Calling a vague intention a project or choosing a heroic scope that cannot survive the first week.

chapters.title: An unconventional education
chapters.sourcePressure: The closing widens ultralearning into learner-built education grounded in projects, adaptation, and responsibility.
chapters.coreMove: Take responsibility for building learning structures without pretending conventional institutions have no value.
chapters.commonMisread: Turning the ending into anti-school manifesto, pure freedom, or career certainty.
